activities.anchor: does the order of decisions make sense
activities.caption: pair each cycle stage with its interaction flavour
activities.name: ixdCycleMatch

config.prompt: The design cycle, run on behaviour — pair each stage:

pairs.right: needfinding — watch tasks and breakdowns, not opinions
requirements as tasks with measurable success criteria
paper flows and Wizard-of-Oz tests of the choreography
the state matrix and flow map engineering can implement unambiguously

config.why: Every stage has a distinct interaction flavour — and the honest unit of requirement is the task, not the feature.

activities.anchor: evaluation is how you learn what to design
activities.caption: bet before the reveal — when does testing run?
activities.name: ixdTestPredict

config.q: A team plans a two-month build followed by a one-week usability test at the end. What does interaction design say about that schedule?
choices: Fine — testing validates the finished design
Evaluation runs at every stage — a Friday paper test can kill a month of wrong development
config.why: Formative tests find comprehension failures early; summative tests compare finished designs on task time, error rate and completion.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the state matrix
activities.name: ixdStateSpot

config.prompt: One of these state claims is backwards — click it:
lines: Focus: a visible ring — the only way a keyboard user knows where they are.
Active: pressed feedback within about 100 ms.
Disabled: grey it out and say nothing — silence is the cleanest choice.
Error: say why the save failed and preserve the user's input.
config.correction: A disabled state with no explanation is a dead end — good practice keeps the button enabled and explains on click what is missing.
config.why: Designing the default alone and shipping it is the single most common quality gap in real products.

activities.anchor: The distinction matters because digital objects have
activities.caption: flat design vs the correction — drag the divider
activities.name: ixdFlatCompare

config.prompt: The signifier's decade of regret — drag between the eras:

before.label: Flat design, 2010s
before.text: Borders, shadows and underlines stripped for minimalism — text that looked like a label became clickable, with measured increases in hesitation and missed targets.

after.label: The correction
after.text: Material's shadows, returned underlines, clearly bordered buttons — not an aesthetic round-trip but a rediscovery that signifiers carry the interaction.

config.why: Every interactive element should answer 'what are you and what happens if I touch you?' before it is touched.

activities.anchor: Motion as pure decoration violates the visual design lesson's clutter principle
activities.caption: place the UI-transition duration
activities.name: ixdMotionPlace

config.prompt: The dosage rule — place a standard UI transition on the milliseconds scale.
config.why: 200–300 ms: fast enough not to feel sluggish, slow enough to be perceived — below roughly 100 ms motion is invisible, above about 500 ms it reads as lag.

activities.anchor: The law's corollaries explain real conventions
activities.caption: call Fitts's prediction
activities.name: ixdFittsEst

config.prompt: With a ≈ 150 ms and b ≈ 150 ms per bit: a pointer moves 200 px to a 40 px-wide button — what movement time does Fitts's law predict?
config.why: ≈ 540 ms — log2(1 + 200/40) ≈ 2.58 bits. Doubling the width to 80 px cuts it to ≈ 420 ms: a 22% saving for a purely geometric decision.
config.context: Screen corners and edges are infinitely deep targets — which is why corner-anchored menus feel so fast.

activities.anchor: progressive disclosure is not just visual hygiene
activities.caption: which curve is Hick's law?
activities.name: ixdHickTrace

config.prompt: Decision time against the entropy of the choice set — which curve is Hick's law?

curves.label: C: flat — choice count is free

config.why: Roughly linear in entropy — so progressive disclosure presenting 3 salient options instead of 15 directly buys back decision time.
